hook: Two lines in his contract cost him $27,000.

scores.worst_problem: The hook promises a specific $27,000 loss but no slide ever delivers that story or number, so the opening curiosity gap is baited and abandoned.
scores.fix: Pay off the hook explicitly on slide 2 by naming the two contract lines and the $27,000 outcome, and swap the flat 'and inspectors are booked solid' loop plus the mismatched keyword TOUR for a tease that withholds (e.g. 'the mistake costs you the window') and a keyword tied to the topic like OPTION.

deck.hook: Two lines in his contract cost him $27,000.

points.title: The Clock Starts Without You
body: A buyer signed on a Friday and mailed his option fee Monday.
By then his window to walk was already dead, and the foundation report came back ugly.
The fee has to be delivered fast or the whole right disappears.
points.loop: most buyers misread what it buys

points.title: You Are Renting Time
body: That fee is not a deposit on the house. It is payment for the right to cancel for any reason at all.
Bad inspection. Cold feet. Nosy neighbour. Does not matter.
points.loop: but the calendar is the trap

points.title: Weekends Still Count
body: These are calendar days, not business days.
Sign on a Thursday and you just burned a chunk of your window on a weekend nobody works.
The deadline hits at a fixed hour on the last day. Not end of day.

points.title: Book Before You Sign
body: Good inspectors run five to eight days out in a busy month.
If you start calling after the contract is executed, you get the report with almost no time left to act on it.
Line up the appointment while the offer is still being negotiated.
points.loop: then most people fumble the ask

points.title: One Ask, Not Three
body: Buyers send a repair request, then remember something, then send another.
Every follow up tells the seller you are emotionally in the house already.
Bundle it. Send once. Give a real deadline.

linkedinCaption:
The Texas option period is the most misunderstood part of a residential contract, and the mistakes are usually procedural rather than strategic.

The fee has to be delivered inside a short window. Late delivery can void the right entirely, regardless of what an inspection later reveals.

Those are calendar days. Weekends count. The deadline lands at a set hour on the final day, not at midnight.

Inspectors in a busy month can book out five to eight days. Scheduling after execution leaves almost no room to act on the findings.

Repair requests should go out once, bundled, with a stated deadline. Multiple rounds signal attachment.

For the agents here: how early in the offer process do you start coordinating the inspection?
